cards.explanation: The answer is True. The proverb says, “A good name is more desirable than great riches…” It even adds that “favor is better than silver and gold.” I'm standing on a gold base as we speak, friends, and I'm telling you the name people know you by outshines it. Gold can't say a kind word about you when you leave the room.

The answer is that the LORD is Maker of them all. The proverb says, “The LORD is Maker of them all.” The rich and the poor can have very different pockets, but they have the same Maker. Nobody gets a fancier label on the back. I like a proverb that levels the whole counter.

The answer is that they take cover. The proverb says, “The prudent see danger and take cover…” They spot it and they move, no speeches. I see a tray of hot cookies sliding off the counter and I do not audition to catch it. The prudent are smarter than me about that kind of thing.

The answer is False. The simple “…keep going and suffer the consequences.” Same danger as the prudent, completely different ending. It's the difference between stepping out of the way and stepping into the whole thing, wearing the apron.

The answer is humility and the fear of the LORD. The proverb says, “The rewards of humility and the fear of the LORD are wealth and honor and life.” Two things go in, three come out. That's a better batch than I've ever baked. Humility I've had plenty of practice with, friends, since I spent years in a junk drawer.

The answer is that he stays far from them, since “…he who guards his soul stays far from them.” He doesn't test how thorny the thorns are. He just keeps his distance. Smart man. I keep my distance from a hot oven door, and my mustache thanks me.

The answer is False. The proverb says, “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” That training sticks all the way to old age. Which is a lot of years of those little lessons staying put.

The answer is slave. The proverb says, “…the borrower is slave to the lender.” That's a heavy word, and the proverb doesn't soften it. When you owe somebody, they hold something over you. I think that's worth remembering next time a payment reminder pops up on your phone.

The answer is disaster. The proverb says, “He who sows injustice will reap disaster…” What gets planted decides what grows. If I plant a flour sack in my kitchen, I don't harvest a bakery. The farming picture makes it easy to see.

The answer is that he shares his bread with the poor. The proverb says, “A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.” The reason is right there in the verse. Bread is the Bible's food here, friends, and I stick to cookies, but I know a good sharing when I see one. His hands were open.

The answer is conflict, friends. The proverb says, “Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart…” The verse goes on: “even quarreling and insults will cease.” One mocker out the door and the whole room breathes again.

The answer is True. The proverb says, “He who loves a pure heart and gracious lips will have the king for a friend.” A pure heart and kind words are the things he loves. A friend with a crown is quite a bonus. I'd take a friend like that over a bigger oven.

The answer is False. The proverb says, “The LORD’s eyes keep watch over knowledge, but He frustrates the words of the faithless.” Their words get frustrated, not helped. His eyes are watching over knowledge, and that's a comforting thing for a stamper to know.

The answer is that there is a lion outside. The slacker says, “There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!” Now that's a dramatic line. I think I'd have to sit down after saying that one. The verse calls the man who says it the slacker.

The answer is he who is under the wrath of the LORD. The proverb says the mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit, and “he who is under the wrath of the LORD will fall into it.” I think this one is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. It's a serious warning, and it's meant to be taken seriously.

The answer is the rod of discipline, friends. The proverb says, “Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.” Discipline is what it names as driving foolishness far away. That's the answer the verse gives. I'm a grown stamper and I still need a little of that now and then.

The answer is poverty. The proverb says, “Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself or giving gifts to the rich will surely lead to poverty.” Squeeze the poor to get rich, or give gifts to the rich, and the verse says either one leads to the same place. Both roads end in poverty. The ending doesn't change.
